young.html: Sigmund Freud (say FROYD) was a doctor in Vienna, Austria, more than a hundred years ago. He listened to people talk about their worries, and he noticed that they often talked about their dreams.

Freud asked a big question: do dreams mean anything? Many people in his time said dreams were just nonsense from a tired brain. Freud thought every dream has a hidden meaning, like a puzzle or a secret code.

Scientists today do not agree with all of Freud's answers. But they agree on one thing you can test yourself: dreams often borrow pieces of your own day, such as a place you visited, a person you talked to, or something you were looking forward to.

young.name: gb-freud-sleep
young.cap: Slide through one night of sleep. Your brain goes through cycles, and the most story-like dreams come in the stage called REM. (A typical pattern, not one person's night.)

young.html: A dream journal. Keep a notebook by your bed for a week. As soon as you wake up, write or draw anything you remember, even one picture. Later in the day, look for links: did anything in the dream come from the day before? Many dreams fade within minutes of waking, so be quick!

full.html: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) grew up in Vienna, trained as a physician, and did research on the nervous system before he turned to treating patients with nervous complaints. In Paris in 1885–86 he watched the neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot at work, and with his Viennese colleague Josef Breuer he published Studies on Hysteria (1895). Out of that work came his "talking cure," which he named psychoanalysis.

The Interpretation of Dreams appeared in November 1899, though the title page says 1900. It sold slowly at first, but Freud always counted it his most important book. A. A. Brill, a New York psychiatrist, made the first English translation in 1913.

Freud begins with a long survey of what earlier writers had said about dreams. Then, in Chapter II, he gives his method and tries it on a dream of his own from July 1895, about a patient he calls Irma. He takes the dream apart piece by piece and writes down whatever comes to mind about each piece. This is free association.

full.text: If the method of dream interpretation here indicated is followed, it will be found that the dream really has meaning, and is by no means the expression of fragmentary brain activity, which the authors would have us believe. When the work of interpretation has been completed the dream may be recognised as the fulfilment of a wish.
full.author: Sigmund Freud
full.work: The Interpretation of Dreams, end of Chapter II

full.html: Freud's reading of his Irma dream (our summary): the dream let him off the hook. It showed that a patient's continuing illness was someone else's fault, not his, which was what he wished.

full.text: Two layers: what you remember and what lies beneath

full.html: Freud separates the dream as you remember it, the manifest content, from the hidden thoughts he looks for beneath it, the latent content. Why the disguise? Freud's answer is a kind of inner censorship: thoughts the dreamer would not accept are allowed through only in disguise.

full.text: We regard the dream thoughts and the dream content as two representations of the same meaning in two different languages; or to express it better, the dream content appears to us as a translation of the dream thoughts into another form of expression, whose signs and laws of composition we are to learn by comparing the original with the translation.
full.author: Sigmund Freud
full.work: The Interpretation of Dreams, Chapter VI (The Dream-Work)

head: Freud's name
What it does (our summary)
rows: Many dream thoughts are squeezed into one image or one mixed-up person.
The feeling moves from what matters onto some small, unimportant detail.
Ideas are turned into pictures that a dream can show.
The dream is patched into a story that seems to hang together.

full.name: gb-freud-dreamwork
full.cap: An invented, everyday dream, read step by step: first as Freud would, then as many researchers would today.

full.html: In the last chapter Freud builds a model of the mind with conscious, preconscious and unconscious parts. He ends with the sentence the book is most remembered for:

full.text: At any rate the interpretation of dreams is the via regia to a knowledge of the unconscious in the psychic life.
full.author: Sigmund Freud
full.work: The Interpretation of Dreams, Chapter VII

full.html: Via regia is Latin for "royal road," the main highway.

Freud's dream book changed how people talked about the mind, in medicine, literature and everyday speech. Its scientific claims have fared unevenly. In 1953 Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman discovered REM sleep, the stage of sleep most linked with vivid dreams, and dream research moved into sleep laboratories. In 1977 J. Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley proposed that dreams arise as the brain makes a story out of its own signals during REM, a direct challenge to Freud. Large studies of dream reports find that dreams often carry the dreamer's waking concerns, which fits part of Freud's picture, but they do not support the claim that every dream fulfils a wish; many dreams are anxious or plain. The philosopher Karl Popper argued that psychoanalysis could explain any outcome and so could not be tested. Defenders reply that some of Freud's broader ideas, such as mental processes outside awareness, are now widely accepted in other forms. Most researchers today treat the book as a landmark in the history of ideas rather than as current science.

Thinking Freud used a dream dictionary ("a snake always means X"). He mostly worked from the dreamer's own associations, and warned that the same image could mean different things for different people, though he did also discuss some common symbols.

items: Aristotle wrote short works on sleep and dreams, explaining them from the body; Freud quotes him in his opening survey.

Sophocles' Oedipus the King, earlier on this ladder: in this book Freud first sketched what he later called the Oedipus complex, his claim that young children have strong, mixed feelings toward their parents that are later forgotten. It became one of his most disputed ideas, with little support from later research.
William James (the rung before this one in the 19th century) also wrote about parts of the mind outside awareness, but he doubted Freud's methods when they met in 1909.
Freud's later works, the next rung, build the ideas of this book into a full theory of the mind.
Can a method that always finds a meaning ever show that it is wrong?
Why do we forget most dreams within minutes?
How much of what we do happens without our noticing why?
Is a dream a message, a memory, a story the brain tells itself, or something else?

questions: What is the strangest dream you remember? Did any piece of it come from real life?
Why might it be hard to remember dreams once you are fully awake?
Freud thought dreams hide their meaning. Many scientists think they do not. What would help you decide?
Why do you think so many words from Freud ("unconscious," "Freudian slip") are used in everyday talk?
Is it fair to judge an old scientific book by what we know today? What else could we judge it by?
care: Freud wrote for adults, and parts of the book touch adult matters. This rung keeps to his main ideas about dreams, his place in history and how later research judged him, with nothing explicit.
